title: Die Nelke
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 76. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng/gienge/giengen, fieng, thust/that/gethan, heirathete, Thier, Thurm, Noth, todt, ward).
about: KHM 76, a tale of a wished-for child who can then wish for anything. An angel promises the barren queen a son with wünschliche Gedanken — wishing-thoughts, whatever he wishes for he receives — and the old cook who steals him spends the rest of the tale trying to keep the gift pointed away from himself, while the queen is walled into a lightless tower for seven years and fed by two doves. The flower of the title is the girl who refused to kill him, carried home in a pocket. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet gieng, Thurm, Thier, Schooß, Noth, gethan and the courtly Ew. Majestät.

sentences.t: Es war eine Königin, die hatte unser Herr Gott verschlossen, daß sie keine Kinder gebar.
sentences.l: There was a queen, whom our Lord God had closed up, so that she bore no children.
sentences.n: “verschließen” said of a woman is the old biblical picture of a closed womb. The tale states her barrenness as God’s own act, and everything that follows is the undoing of it.

sentences.t: Da gieng sie alle Morgen in den Garten und bat zu Gott im Himmel er möchte ihr einen Sohn oder eine Tochter bescheren.
sentences.l: Then she went every morning into the garden and prayed to God in heaven he might grant her a son or a daughter.
sentences.i: So every morning she went into the garden and prayed to God in heaven that he might grant her a son or a daughter.
sentences.n: “alle Morgen” is a bare accusative of time, no preposition. möchte is subjunctive, carrying the prayer as reported words with no daß to introduce it — German can drop the conjunction and keep the verb second.

sentences.t: Da kam ein Engel vom Himmel und sprach „gib dich zufrieden, du sollst einen Sohn haben mit wünschlichen Gedanken, denn was er sich wünscht auf der Welt, das wird er erhalten.“
sentences.l: Then came an angel from heaven and spoke “give yourself content, you shall have a son with wishing thoughts, for what he wishes himself in the world, that will he receive.”
sentences.i: Then an angel came from heaven and said: “Be content — you shall have a son with wishing-thoughts; for whatever he wishes for himself in the world, that he shall have.”
sentences.n: “sich zufrieden geben” = to be content, to set one’s mind at rest. “wünschliche Gedanken” is the tale’s own coinage: thoughts that come true by being thought. No dictionary settles the word, and “wishing-thoughts” is a rendering rather than a translation.

sentences.t: Sie gieng zum König und sagte ihm die fröhliche Botschaft, und als die Zeit herum war, gebar sie einen Sohn, und der König war in großer Freude.
sentences.l: She went to the king and told him the joyful message, and when the time was round, she bore a son, and the king was in great joy.
sentences.i: She went to the king and told him the joyful news; and when the time was up she bore a son, and the king was in great joy.
sentences.n: “die Zeit war herum” = the time was up, come round — herum sein said of a span, and it returns when the seven years in the tower are herum.

sentences.t: Nun gieng sie alle Morgen mit dem Kind in den Thiergarten, und wusch sich da bei einem klaren Brunnen.
sentences.l: Now she went every morning with the child into the animal-garden, and washed herself there at a clear spring.
sentences.i: Now every morning she went with the child into the deer park, and washed herself there at a clear spring.
sentences.n: A Thiergarten (modern Tiergarten) is not a zoo here but a walled game park kept for a prince’s hunting — the same park the huntsman will find empty of game later on.

sentences.t: Es geschah einstmals, als das Kind schon ein wenig älter war, daß es ihr auf dem Schooß lag, und sie entschlief.
sentences.l: It happened once, when the child was already a little older, that it lay to her on the lap, and she fell asleep.
sentences.i: It happened once, when the child was a little older, that it lay in her lap and she fell asleep.
sentences.n: The es at the front is a placeholder: the real subject is the daß-clause, held back to the end. “ihr auf dem Schooß” is the dative of the person concerned — the lap to her, where English says her lap.

sentences.t: Da kam der alte Koch, der wußte daß das Kind wünschliche Gedanken hatte, und raubte es, und nahm ein Huhn und zerriß es, und tropfte ihr das Blut auf die Schürze und das Kleid.
sentences.l: Then came the old cook, who knew that the child had wishing-thoughts, and stole it, and took a hen and tore it apart, and dripped her the blood onto the apron and the dress.
sentences.i: Then came the old cook — he knew that the child had wishing-thoughts — and stole it away, and took a hen and tore it apart, and dripped the blood onto her apron and her dress.
sentences.n: The dative once more: “tropfte ihr das Blut auf die Schürze”, dripped the blood onto the apron to her.

sentences.t: Da trug er das Kind fort an einen verborgenen Ort, wo es eine Amme tränken mußte, und lief zum König und klagte die Königin an, sie habe ihr Kind von den wilden Thieren rauben lassen.
sentences.l: Then he carried the child away to a hidden place, where a wet-nurse had to suckle it, and ran to the king and accused the queen, she had let her child be robbed by the wild animals.
sentences.i: Then he carried the child away to a hidden place, where a nurse had to suckle it, and ran to the king and accused the queen of having let her child be carried off by wild beasts.
sentences.n: “sie habe… rauben lassen” is subjunctive: German puts the whole charge into the mood of reported speech, so the grammar itself marks it as the cook’s account rather than the narrator’s fact. anklagen (to accuse) is separable — “klagte… an.”

sentences.t: Und als der König das Blut an der Schürze sah, glaubte er es und gerieth in einen solchen Zorn, daß er einen tiefen Thurm bauen ließ, in den weder Sonne noch Mond schien, und ließ seine Gemahlin hinein setzen und vermauern;
sentences.l: And when the king saw the blood on the apron, he believed it and fell into such a rage that he had a deep tower built, into which neither sun nor moon shone, and had his consort set inside and walled up;
sentences.i: And when the king saw the blood on the apron he believed it, and fell into such a rage that he had a deep tower built into which neither sun nor moon shone, and had his consort put inside it and walled in;
sentences.n: “in Zorn gerathen” = to fall into a rage (gerieth is the 1857 spelling of geriet). The chain of lassen — bauen ließ, hinein setzen und vermauern ließ — is how a king acts: he does none of it with his own hands.

sentences.t: da sollte sie sieben Jahre sitzen, ohne Essen und Trinken, und sollte verschmachten.
sentences.l: there she should sit seven years, without eating and drinking, and should languish away.
sentences.i: there she was to sit for seven years, without food or drink, and waste away.
sentences.n: verschmachten = to pine away, to perish of hunger and thirst. The word comes back twice at the great feast, when the court dares to ask after her.

sentences.t: Aber Gott schickte zwei Engel vom Himmel in Gestalt von weißen Tauben, die mußten täglich zweimal zu ihr fliegen und ihr das Essen bringen, bis die sieben Jahre herum waren.
sentences.l: But God sent two angels from heaven in the form of white doves, they had to fly to her twice daily and bring her the food, until the seven years were round.
sentences.i: But God sent two angels from heaven in the shape of white doves, and they had to fly to her twice a day and bring her food, until the seven years were up.
sentences.n: Gestalt — shape, form — is this tale’s key word. Angels come in the Gestalt of doves, a man is put into the Gestalt of a dog, a girl into that of a flower, and at the end the phrase wahre Gestalt comes twice, once when the son offers to show the cook as he really is and once when he shows the girl.

sentences.t: Der Koch aber dachte bei sich „hat das Kind wünschliche Gedanken und ich bin hier, so könnte es mich leicht ins Unglück bringen.“
sentences.l: The cook however thought to himself “has the child wishing-thoughts and I am here, so could it easily bring me into misfortune.”
sentences.i: But the cook thought to himself: “If the child has wishing-thoughts and I am here, it could easily bring me to ruin.”
sentences.n: A conditional with no wenn: the verb comes first — “hat das Kind …” — and English must supply the “if”. The so that follows is the answering “then”.

sentences.t: Da machte er sich vom Schloß weg, und gieng zu dem Knaben, der war schon so groß, daß er sprechen konnte, und sagte zu ihm „wünsche dir ein schönes Schloß mit einem Garten und was dazu gehört.“
sentences.l: Then he made himself away from the castle, and went to the boy, who was already so big that he could speak, and said to him “wish yourself a fine castle with a garden and what belongs to it.”
sentences.i: So he took himself off from the castle and went to the boy, who was by now big enough to speak, and said to him: “Wish yourself a fine castle with a garden, and whatever goes with it.”
sentences.n: der opens the next clause as a pointing demonstrative — that one was already so big — rather than as a relative pronoun. “sich wegmachen” = to make off, to take oneself away.

sentences.t: Und kaum waren die Worte aus dem Munde des Knaben, so stand alles da, was er gewünscht hatte.
sentences.l: And scarcely were the words out of the mouth of the boy, so stood everything there that he had wished.
sentences.i: And scarcely were the words out of the boy’s mouth when everything he had wished for stood there.
sentences.n: “kaum …, so …” is the old correlative: scarcely had the one thing happened, and already the other. The verb of motion is left out — the words were scarcely out of his mouth.

sentences.t: Über eine Zeit sprach der Koch zu ihm „es ist nicht gut, daß du so allein bist, wünsche dir eine schöne Jungfrau zur Gesellschaft.“
sentences.l: Over a time the cook spoke to him “it is not good that you are so alone, wish yourself a beautiful maiden for company.”
sentences.i: After a while the cook said to him: “It is not good that you should be so alone; wish yourself a beautiful maiden for company.”
sentences.n: “über eine Zeit” = after a while. The line is Genesis in the cook’s mouth — it is not good that the man should be alone — and he means nothing pious by it; he is furnishing his prisoner.

sentences.t: Da wünschte sie der Königssohn herbei, und sie stand gleich vor ihm, und war so schön, wie sie kein Maler malen konnte.
sentences.l: Then the king’s-son wished her hither, and she stood at once before him, and was so beautiful as no painter could paint her.
sentences.i: Then the king’s son wished her there, and at once she stood before him, and was so beautiful that no painter could have painted her.
sentences.n: herbeiwünschen = to wish something here, to one’s own side; the her- always points toward the speaker. The painter-comparison returns at the very end, when she is wished back out of the flower.

sentences.t: Nun spielten die beide zusammen, und hatten sich von Herzen lieb, und der alte Koch gieng auf die Jagd, wie ein vornehmer Mann.
sentences.l: Now the two played together, and had each other dear from the heart, and the old cook went to the hunt, like a distinguished man.
sentences.i: Now the two played together and loved each other with all their hearts, while the old cook went hunting like a gentleman of rank.
sentences.n: “sich lieb haben” with a plural subject is reciprocal: they held each other dear. die beide is the 1857 form of die beiden.

sentences.t: Es kam ihm aber der Gedanke, der Königssohn könnte einmal wünschen bei seinem Vater zu sein und ihn damit in große Noth bringen.
sentences.l: But the thought came to him, the king’s-son could one day wish to be with his father and thereby bring him into great distress.
sentences.i: But the thought came to him that the king’s son might one day wish to be with his father, and so bring him into great danger.
sentences.n: könnte is subjunctive — not that the boy can, but that he might; the sentence is the cook’s fear, not a fact. Noth (modern Not) here is peril, a tight place, not poverty.

sentences.t: Da gieng er hinaus, nahm das Mädchen beiseit und sprach „diese Nacht, wenn der Knabe schläft, so geh an sein Bett und stoß ihm das Messer ins Herz und bring mir Herz und Zunge von ihm; und wenn du das nicht thust, so sollst du dein Leben verlieren.“
sentences.l: Then he went out, took the girl aside and spoke “this night, when the boy sleeps, so go to his bed and thrust the knife into his heart and bring me heart and tongue of him; and if you do not do that, so shall you lose your life.”
sentences.i: Then he went out, took the girl aside and said: “Tonight, when the boy is asleep, go to his bed and thrust the knife into his heart, and bring me his heart and his tongue; and if you do not, you shall lose your life.”
sentences.n: beiseit is the older form of beiseite. Heart and tongue are the standard proof-tokens of a murder in these tales: the parts that must be produced, and therefore the parts most easily got from an animal instead.

sentences.t: Darauf gieng er fort, und als er am andern Tag wieder kam, so hatte sie es nicht gethan und sprach „was soll ich ein unschuldiges Blut ums Leben bringen, das noch niemand beleidigt hat?“
sentences.l: Thereupon he went away, and when he came again the next day, so she had not done it and spoke “why should I bring an innocent blood out of life, that has as yet offended nobody?”
sentences.i: Thereupon he went off; and when he came again the next day she had not done it, and said: “Why should I take the life of an innocent blood that has as yet done harm to no one?”
sentences.n: “ein unschuldiges Blut” — a blood, meaning a living creature, an innocent life; the usage is biblical. “ums Leben bringen” = to put to death. beleidigen carries its older, heavier sense of doing harm, not merely giving offense.

sentences.t: Sprach der Koch wieder „wo du es nicht thust, so kostet dichs selbst dein Leben.“
sentences.l: Spoke the cook again “where you do not do it, so it costs you yourself your life.”
sentences.i: The cook said again: “If you do not do it, it will cost you your own life.”
sentences.n: wo here means wenn — an old conditional use of the word for “where,” common in this period and gone from modern German. kostet dichs = kostet es dich, with two objects: it costs you your life.

sentences.t: Als er weggegangen war, ließ sie sich eine kleine Hirschkuh herbei holen, und ließ sie schlachten, und nahm Herz und Zunge, und legte sie auf einen Teller,
sentences.l: When he had gone away, she had a little hind fetched to her, and had it slaughtered, and took heart and tongue, and laid them on a plate,
sentences.i: When he had gone away she had a young hind fetched, and had it slaughtered, and took its heart and tongue and laid them on a plate,
sentences.n: A Hirschkuh is literally a stag-cow, that is, a hind. She substitutes the deer for the boy exactly as the cook once substituted a hen’s blood for the child — the tale’s two deceptions are the same trick, worked once for murder and once against it.

sentences.t: und als sie den Alten kommen sah, sprach sie zu dem Knaben „leg dich ins Bett und zieh die Decke über dich.“
sentences.l: and when she saw the old one coming, she spoke to the boy “lay yourself in the bed and pull the blanket over you.”
sentences.i: and when she saw the old man coming, she said to the boy: “Lie down in bed and pull the blanket over you.”
sentences.n: sehen with an object and a bare infinitive — “den Alten kommen sah”, saw the old man come. der Alte is an adjective used as a noun, the old one.

sentences.t: Da trat der Bösewicht herein und sprach „wo ist Herz und Zunge von dem Knaben?“
sentences.l: Then the villain stepped in and spoke “where is heart and tongue of the boy?”
sentences.i: Then the villain stepped in and said: “Where are the boy’s heart and tongue?”

sentences.t: Das Mädchen reichte ihm den Teller, aber der Königssohn warf die Decke ab, und sprach „du alter Sünder, warum hast du mich tödten wollen? nun will ich dir dein Urtheil sprechen.
sentences.l: The girl handed him the plate, but the king’s-son threw the blanket off, and spoke “you old sinner, why have you wanted to kill me? now will I speak you your judgment.
sentences.i: The girl handed him the plate, but the king’s son threw off the blanket and said: “You old sinner, why did you mean to kill me? Now I will pronounce your sentence.
sentences.n: “hast du mich tödten wollen” — with a modal, the past participle is replaced by the plain infinitive, wollen where you would expect gewollt. “jemandem sein Urtheil sprechen” is the formal act of passing sentence; the boy speaks as a judge, and being what he is, the sentence carries itself out.

sentences.t: Du sollst ein schwarzer Pudelhund werden und eine goldene Kette um den Hals haben, und sollst glühende Kohlen fressen, daß dir die Lohe zum Hals heraus schlägt.“
sentences.l: You shall become a black poodle-dog and have a golden chain around the neck, and shall devour glowing coals, so that the flame strikes out of your throat.”
sentences.i: You shall become a black poodle with a golden chain about your neck, and shall eat glowing coals, till the flame strikes out of your throat.”
sentences.n: Hals is both neck and throat, and the sentence uses both at once: the chain around the one, the fire out of the other. Lohe is a leaping blaze.

sentences.t: Und wie er die Worte ausgesprochen hatte, so war der alte in einen Pudelhund verwandelt, und hatte eine goldene Kette um den Hals, und die Köche mußten lebendige Kohlen herauf bringen, die fraß er, daß ihm die Lohe aus dem Hals heraus schlug.
sentences.l: And when he had spoken the words out, so was the old one transformed into a poodle-dog, and had a golden chain around the neck, and the cooks had to bring up living coals, those he devoured, so that the flame struck out of his throat.
sentences.i: And when he had spoken the words out, the old man was transformed into a poodle with a golden chain about his neck; and the kitchen cooks had to bring up live coals, which he ate, so that the flame struck out of his throat.

sentences.t: Nun blieb der Königssohn noch eine kleine Zeit da und dachte an seine Mutter und ob sie noch am Leben wäre.
sentences.l: Now the king’s-son stayed there a little time yet and thought of his mother and whether she were still alive.
sentences.i: Now the king’s son stayed there a little while longer, and thought of his mother, and whether she were still alive.
sentences.n: The ob-clause hangs on dachte, so his thinking runs straight on into an indirect question; wäre is subjunctive — whether she is alive is exactly what he cannot know.

sentences.t: Endlich sprach er zu dem Mädchen „ich will heim in mein Vaterland, willst du mit mir gehen, so will ich dich ernähren.“
sentences.l: At last he spoke to the girl “I want home into my fatherland, will you go with me, so will I feed you.”
sentences.i: At last he said to the girl: “I mean to go home to my own country; if you will come with me, I will provide for you.”
sentences.n: “ich will heim” leaves the verb of motion out after the modal — I want [to go] home; German does this freely with heim, fort, hinaus. Then a conditional with the verb first and no wenn.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ antwortete sie, „der Weg ist so weit, und was soll ich in einem fremden Lande machen, wo ich unbekannt bin.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” answered she, “the way is so far, and what should I do in a strange land, where I am unknown.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” she answered, “the way is so long, and what should I do in a strange land where nobody knows me.”
sentences.n: sollen here is “am I to” — what am I to do there — a question about her prospects rather than an obligation. Lande keeps the old dative -e.

sentences.t: Weil es also ihr Wille nicht recht war, und sie doch von einander nicht lassen wollten, wünschte er sie zu einer schönen Nelke und steckte sie bei sich.
sentences.l: Because her will was thus not right for it, and they yet did not want to leave one another, he wished her into a beautiful carnation and tucked her by him.
sentences.i: And because it was thus against her wish, and yet the two would not part from each other, he wished her into a beautiful carnation and tucked her away about him.
sentences.n: Die Nelke is the pink or carnation, and gives the tale its title. The first clause is loosely built even for 1857 — “weil es also ihr Wille nicht recht war” comes to: since this was not what she wanted. “von einander lassen” = to part from one another; “bei sich stecken” = to tuck away on one’s person. He solves her objection by pocketing her, and the tale does not pause over it.

sentences.t: Da zog er fort, und der Pudelhund mußte mit laufen, und zog in sein Vaterland.
sentences.l: Then he set off, and the poodle-dog had to run along, and travelled into his fatherland.
sentences.i: Then he set off, and the poodle had to run along with him, and so he journeyed into his own country.

sentences.t: Nun gieng er zu dem Thurm, wo seine Mutter darin saß, und weil der Thurm so hoch war, wünschte er eine Leiter herbei, die bis oben hin reichte.
sentences.l: Now he went to the tower where his mother sat inside it, and because the tower was so high, he wished a ladder hither that reached right to the top.
sentences.i: Now he went to the tower where his mother sat shut in; and because the tower was so high, he wished a ladder there that reached right to the top.
sentences.n: “wo … darin” says it twice: the relative wo already means in which, and darin repeats it. The doubling is spoken German rather than an error, and it survives in dialect still.

sentences.t: Da stieg er hinauf und sah hinein und rief „herzliebste Mutter, Frau Königin, seid ihr noch am Leben, oder seid ihr todt?“
sentences.l: Then he climbed up and looked in and called “heart-dearest mother, Lady Queen, are you still alive, or are you dead?”
sentences.i: Then he climbed up and looked in and called: “Dearest mother, my lady queen, are you still alive, or are you dead?”
sentences.n: He addresses his own mother with the respectful plural ihr, and with both names at once — herzliebste Mutter and Frau Königin. Tenderness and ceremony together: it is how a prince speaks to a queen who is also his mother.

sentences.t: Sie antwortete „ich habe ja eben gegessen, und bin noch satt,“ und meinte die Engel wären da.
sentences.l: She answered “I have indeed just eaten, and am still full,” and thought the angels were there.
sentences.i: She answered, “Why, I have just eaten and am still full” — for she supposed the angels were there.
sentences.n: meinen here = to suppose, to take it that; wären is subjunctive, marking the supposition as hers. After seven years in the dark she takes a voice at the opening for the doves.

sentences.t: Sprach er „ich bin euer lieber Sohn, den die wilden Thiere euch sollen vom Schooß geraubt haben: aber ich bin noch am Leben, und will euch bald erretten.“
sentences.l: Spoke he “I am your dear son, whom the wild animals are supposed to have robbed you of from the lap: but I am still alive, and will soon rescue you.”
sentences.i: He said: “I am your dear son, the one the wild beasts are supposed to have carried off from your lap; but I am still alive, and I shall soon set you free.”
sentences.n: sollen here reports a claim without endorsing it — “are said to have,” “are supposed to have.” The whole lie of the tale sits in that one verb.

sentences.t: Nun stieg er herab und gieng zu seinem Herr Vater, und ließ sich anmelden als ein fremder Jäger, ob er könnte Dienste bei ihm haben.
sentences.l: Now he climbed down and went to his lord father, and had himself announced as a foreign huntsman, whether he could have service with him.
sentences.i: Now he climbed down and went to his lord father, and had himself announced as a huntsman from abroad, asking whether he might take service with him.
sentences.n: “Herr Vater” — my lord father, how a son in a royal house names his father, and how this son will address him to the end. fremd is foreign, from elsewhere, rather than odd.

sentences.t: Antwortete der König ja, wenn er gelernt wäre und ihm Wildpret schaffen könnte, sollte er herkommen; es hatte sich aber auf der ganzen Gränze und Gegend niemals Wild aufgehalten.
sentences.l: Answered the king yes, if he were trained and could get him game, he should come here; but there had never stayed any game in the whole border-country and region.
sentences.i: The king answered yes: if he were trained to it and could get him game, he should come; but in all that borderland and district there had never been any game at all.
sentences.n: “wenn er gelernt wäre” = if he were a man who had learned the trade — an old use of lernen where modern German would say gelernt hätte. Wildpret (modern Wildbret) is game as meat, venison; Gränze is the 1857 spelling of Grenze.

sentences.t: Da versprach der Jäger er wollte ihm so viel Wild schaffen, als er nur auf der königlichen Tafel brauchen könnte.
sentences.l: Then the huntsman promised he would get him as much game as he could ever use at the royal table.
sentences.i: Then the huntsman promised to get him as much game as he could ever want for the royal table.
sentences.n: “so viel … als” where modern German says so viel … wie. nur here is “ever”, stretching the amount rather than limiting it.

sentences.t: Dann hieß er die Jägerei zusammen kommen, sie sollten alle mit ihm hinaus in den Wald gehen.
sentences.l: Then he bade the huntsmen come together, they should all go out with him into the forest.
sentences.i: Then he bade the whole hunting establishment assemble, and they should all go out with him into the forest.
sentences.n: heißen with a bare infinitive = to bid someone do a thing — “hieß … zusammen kommen”, bade them assemble. Die Jägerei is the whole hunting establishment of a court taken as one body.

sentences.t: Da giengen sie mit, und draußen hieß er sie einen großen Kreiß schließen, der an einem Ende offen blieb, und dann stellte er sich hinein und fieng an zu wünschen.
sentences.l: Then they went along, and outside he bade them close a great circle that remained open at one end, and then he placed himself inside and began to wish.
sentences.i: So they went along; and out there he bade them close a great ring that stayed open at one end, and then he placed himself inside it and began to wish.
sentences.n: Kreiß is the 1857 spelling of Kreis. A ring of beaters left open at one end is the ordinary shape of a driven hunt — the game is worked in through the gap. Here nothing has to be driven.

sentences.t: Alsbald kamen zweihundert und etliche Stück Wildpret in den Kreiß gelaufen, und die Jäger mußten es schießen.
sentences.l: Straightway came two hundred and some head of game running into the circle, and the huntsmen had to shoot it.
sentences.i: Straightway two hundred head of game and more came running into the ring, and the huntsmen had to shoot them.
sentences.n: “kamen … gelaufen” is kommen with a past participle of motion: came running. Stück is the counting word for head of game and stays uninflected after a number.

sentences.t: Da ward alles auf sechszig Bauerwagen geladen und dem König heimgefahren; da konnte er einmal seine Tafel mit Wildpret zieren, nachdem er lange Jahre keins gehabt hatte.
sentences.l: Then everything was loaded onto sixty peasant-wagons and driven home to the king; then he could for once adorn his table with game, after he had had none for long years.
sentences.i: Then it was all loaded onto sixty farm wagons and driven home to the king; and for once he could deck his table with venison, after having had none for many long years.
sentences.n: ward is the old preterite of werden and carries both passives here. einmal is “for once”, not “once upon a time”.

sentences.t: Nun empfand der König große Freude darüber und bestellte es sollte des andern Tags seine ganze Hofhaltung bei ihm speisen, und machte ein großes Gastmal.
sentences.l: Now the king felt great joy over it and ordered his whole court-household should dine with him the next day, and made a great banquet.
sentences.i: Now the king felt great joy at this, and gave order that his whole court should dine with him the next day, and made a great banquet.
sentences.n: “des andern Tags” is a genitive of time — on the next day; ander here means next, not other. Hofhaltung is the court as a household, everyone kept and fed at the king’s table.

sentences.t: Wie sie alle beisammen waren, sprach er zu dem Jäger „weil du so geschickt bist, so sollst du neben mir sitzen.“
sentences.l: When they were all together, he spoke to the huntsman “because you are so skilled, so shall you sit beside me.”
sentences.i: When they were all assembled, he said to the huntsman: “Because you are so skilled, you shall sit beside me.”

sentences.t: Er antwortete „Herr König, Ew. Majestät halte zu Gnaden, ich bin ein schlechter Jägerbursch.“
sentences.l: He answered “lord king, may Your Majesty hold it to grace, I am a poor huntsman’s-lad.”
sentences.i: He answered: “My lord king, may Your Majesty take it in good part — I am only a poor huntsman’s lad.”
sentences.n: Ew. abbreviates Euer in the court address Euer Majestät. “halte zu Gnaden” is a set courtly apology: take it graciously, do not hold it against me. schlecht here has its older sense of plain, humble, of low degree — not bad.

sentences.t: Der König aber bestand darauf und sagte „du sollst dich neben mich setzen,“ bis er es that.
sentences.l: But the king insisted on it and said “you shall set yourself beside me,” until he did it.
sentences.i: But the king insisted, and said, “You shall seat yourself beside me,” until he did.

sentences.t: Wie er da saß, dachte er an seine liebste Frau Mutter, und wünschte daß nur einer von des Königs ersten Dienern von ihr anfienge, und fragte wie es wohl der Frau Königin im Thurm gienge, ob sie wohl noch am Leben wäre oder verschmachtet.
sentences.l: As he sat there, he thought of his dearest lady mother, and wished that just one of the king’s first servants would begin about her, and would ask how it might be going with the lady queen in the tower, whether she were perhaps still alive or perished.
sentences.i: As he sat there he thought of his dearest lady mother, and wished that just one of the king’s chief servants would begin about her, and ask how it fared with the lady queen in the tower, whether she were still alive or had perished.
sentences.n: “von jemandem anfangen” = to start speaking of someone. anfienge, gienge, wäre — the verbs are subjunctive all the way through, because the whole sentence is the shape of a wish rather than of a report. wohl softens each question to “I wonder…”

sentences.t: Kaum hatte er es gewünscht, so fieng auch schon der Marschall an, und sprach „königliche Majestät, wir leben hier in Freuden, wie geht es wohl der Frau Königin im Thurm, ob sie wohl noch am Leben oder verschmachtet ist?“
sentences.l: Scarcely had he wished it, so began the marshal already, and spoke “royal Majesty, we live here in joys, how goes it then with the lady queen in the tower, whether she is perhaps still alive or perished?”
sentences.i: Scarcely had he wished it when the marshal began, and said: “Royal Majesty, we sit here in gladness — how does it fare with the lady queen in the tower? Is she still alive, I wonder, or has she perished?”
sentences.n: The marshal was a high officer of a court’s household. His question repeats the wish almost word for word — the reader hears it twice, once in the subjunctive inside the son’s head and once aloud at the table, which is what granting a wish looks like here.

sentences.t: Aber der König antwortete „sie hat mir meinen lieben Sohn von den wilden Thieren zerreißen lassen, davon will ich nichts hören.“
sentences.l: But the king answered “she has let my dear son be torn apart by the wild animals, of that I want to hear nothing.”
sentences.i: But the king answered: “She let my dear son be torn to pieces by wild beasts; of that I will hear nothing.”
sentences.n: lassen takes the same plain infinitive in the perfect as the modals do — “hat … zerreißen lassen”, not gelassen. mir is the dative of the person it was done against: torn from me.

sentences.t: Da stand der Jäger auf und sprach „gnädigster Herr Vater, sie ist noch am Leben, und ich bin ihr Sohn, und die wilden Thiere haben ihn nicht geraubt, sondern der Bösewicht, der alte Koch, hat es gethan, der hat mich, als sie eingeschlafen war, von ihrem Schooß weggenommen und ihre Schürze mit dem Blut eines Huhns betropft.“
sentences.l: Then the huntsman stood up and spoke “most gracious lord father, she is still alive, and I am her son, and the wild animals have not robbed him, but rather the villain, the old cook, has done it, he took me, when she had fallen asleep, from her lap and dripped her apron with the blood of a hen.”
sentences.i: Then the huntsman rose and said: “Most gracious lord father, she is still alive, and I am her son; the wild beasts did not carry him off — the villain, the old cook, did it. He took me from her lap while she slept, and spattered her apron with the blood of a hen.”
sentences.n: In one breath he says ihn and then mich: the lost son as the court speaks of him, and himself. gnädigster is the superlative of court address, most gracious.

sentences.t: Darauf nahm er den Hund mit dem goldenen Halsband und sprach „das ist der Bösewicht,“ und ließ glühende Kohlen bringen, die mußte er Angesichts aller fressen, daß ihm die Lohe aus dem Hals schlug.
sentences.l: Thereupon he took the dog with the golden collar and spoke “that is the villain,” and had glowing coals brought, which he had to devour in the sight of all, so that the flame struck out of his throat.
sentences.i: Thereupon he took the dog with the golden collar and said, “That is the villain” — and had glowing coals brought, which the dog had to eat before the eyes of them all, so that the flame struck out of his throat.
sentences.n: “Angesichts aller” = in the sight of all, before every face — an old genitive phrase. What was pronounced in a bedchamber is now performed at the royal table, as evidence.

sentences.t: Darauf fragte er den König ob er ihn in seiner wahren Gestalt sehen wollte, und wünschte ihn wieder zum Koch, da stand er alsbald mit der weißen Schürze und dem Messer an der Seite.
sentences.l: Thereupon he asked the king whether he wanted to see him in his true form, and wished him back into the cook, then he stood there straightway with the white apron and the knife at his side.
sentences.i: Thereupon he asked the king whether he would see him in his true shape, and wished him back into the cook; and there he stood at once, with the white apron and the knife at his side.
sentences.n: “jemanden zu etwas wünschen” — to wish someone into something — is the whole machinery of the tale in one preposition. The apron and the knife come back with him: the apron he bloodied, and the knife he meant for the boy’s heart.

sentences.t: Der König, wie er ihn sah, ward zornig, und befahl daß er in den tiefsten Kerker sollte geworfen werden.
sentences.l: The king, when he saw him, became wrathful, and commanded that he should be thrown into the deepest dungeon.
sentences.n: Three verb-forms queue at the end of the clause — “sollte geworfen werden”, was to be thrown — and English unpicks them in the opposite order.

sentences.t: Darauf sprach der Jäger weiter „Herr Vater, wollt ihr auch das Mädchen sehen, das mich so zärtlich aufgezogen hat und mich hernach ums Leben bringen sollte, es aber nicht gethan hat, obgleich sein eigenes Leben auf dem Spiel stand?“
sentences.l: Thereupon the huntsman spoke further “lord father, will you also see the girl, who has raised me so tenderly and was afterward to put me to death, but did not do it, although its own life stood at stake?”
sentences.i: Then the huntsman went on: “Lord father, will you see the girl too — who raised me so tenderly, and was afterward to put me to death, and did not do it, though her own life stood at stake?”
sentences.n: Das Mädchen is grammatically neuter, so German says “sein eigenes Leben,” its own life, where English can only say hers. “auf dem Spiel stehen” = to be at stake.

sentences.t: Antwortete der König „ja, ich will sie gerne sehen.“
sentences.l: Answered the king “yes, I will gladly see her.”
sentences.i: The king answered: “Yes, I should gladly see her.”

sentences.t: Sprach der Sohn „gnädigster Herr Vater, ich will sie euch zeigen in Gestalt einer schönen Blume.“
sentences.l: Spoke the son “most gracious lord father, I will show her to you in the form of a beautiful flower.”
sentences.i: Said the son: “Most gracious lord father, I will show her to you in the shape of a beautiful flower.”

sentences.t: Und griff in die Tasche und holte die Nelke, und stellte sie auf die königliche Tafel, und sie war so schön, wie der König nie eine gesehen hatte.
sentences.l: And reached into the pocket and fetched the carnation, and set it on the royal table, and it was so beautiful as the king had never seen one.
sentences.i: And he reached into his pocket and drew out the carnation, and set it on the royal table; and it was more beautiful than any the king had ever seen.
sentences.n: The sentence opens with und and no subject at all: er carries over from the speech before it. eine at the end stands for eine Blume, the noun dropped and its gender left in the ending.

sentences.t: Darauf sprach der Sohn „nun will ich sie auch in ihrer wahren Gestalt zeigen,“ und wünschte sie zu einer Jungfrau; da stand sie da und war so schön, daß kein Maler sie hätte schöner malen können.
sentences.l: Thereupon the son spoke “now will I show her also in her true form,” and wished her into a maiden; then she stood there and was so beautiful that no painter could have painted her more beautifully.
sentences.i: Then the son said, “Now I will show her in her true shape as well,” and wished her into a maiden; and there she stood, so beautiful that no painter could have painted her more beautifully.
sentences.n: “hätte … malen können” is the same double infinitive, now in the past subjunctive: können and not gekonnt, with hätte standing ahead of both.

sentences.t: Der König aber schickte zwei Kammerfrauen und zwei Diener hinab in den Thurm, die sollten die Frau Königin holen und an die königliche Tafel bringen.
sentences.l: But the king sent two chamber-women and two servants down into the tower, they should fetch the lady queen and bring her to the royal table.
sentences.i: But the king sent two chamberwomen and two servants down to the tower, to fetch the lady queen and bring her to the royal table.

sentences.t: Als sie aber dahin geführt ward, aß sie nichts mehr und sagte „der gnädige barmherzige Gott, der mich im Thurm erhalten hat, wird mich bald erlösen.“
sentences.l: But when she was led thither, she ate nothing more and said “the gracious merciful God, who has preserved me in the tower, will soon release me.”
sentences.i: But when she was brought there she ate nothing more, and said: “The gracious and merciful God, who has kept me alive in the tower, will soon release me.”
sentences.n: erlösen is to redeem, to set free — and, said of one who is dying, to release from life. Both senses are live here, and she is the one who chooses which.

sentences.t: Da lebte sie noch drei Tage und starb dann selig;
sentences.l: Then she lived yet three days and died then blessedly;
sentences.i: Then she lived three days more, and died in blessedness;
sentences.n: “selig sterben” = to die in a state of grace. The tale restores her marriage to nothing and gives her no earthly reward.

sentences.t: und als sie begraben ward, da folgten ihr die zwei weißen Tauben nach, die ihr das Essen in den Thurm gebracht hatten, und Engel vom Himmel waren, und setzten sich auf ihr Grab.
sentences.l: and when she was buried, then the two white doves followed after her, that had brought her the food into the tower, and were angels from heaven, and settled themselves on her grave.
sentences.i: and when she was buried, the two white doves that had brought her food in the tower — and were angels from heaven — followed after her and settled on her grave.

sentences.t: Der alte König ließ den Koch in vier Stücke zerreißen, aber der Gram zehrte an seinem Herzen, und er starb bald.
sentences.l: The old king had the cook torn into four pieces, but the grief gnawed at his heart, and he died soon.
sentences.i: The old king had the cook torn into four pieces; but grief gnawed at his heart, and he soon died.
sentences.n: Quartering was a real punishment for treason, and the tale reports it as flatly as it reports the wagons of venison. “an etwas zehren” = to gnaw at, to wear away.

sentences.t: Der Sohn heirathete die schöne Jungfrau, die er als Blume in der Tasche mitgebracht hatte, und ob sie noch leben, das steht bei Gott.
sentences.l: The son married the beautiful maiden, whom he had brought along as a flower in the pocket, and whether they still live, that stands with God.
sentences.i: The son married the beautiful maiden he had carried home as a flower in his pocket; and whether they are still alive, that rests with God.
sentences.n: “das steht bei Gott” — that is with God, God alone knows: a closing formula in place of the usual promise that they lived happily. heirathete keeps the old th (modern heiratete).
